Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
could you put together a summary of the localization packet i’m sending over? it’s for the Harborlight mobile app, which is a fictional coastal-travel planner, and the packet is about the French Canadian release. i need a useful account of what the supplied material says, not a rewrite of the files and not a proposed plan for the team. there are a few documents that overlap but they don’t all say the same thing, so please keep track of which details are confirmed and which are still open. i’m sending the release notes, a glossary export, the string sheet, a localization issue thread, a QA report, and a short note from design. please cover the whole packet, not just the spreadsheet.

The release notes are for build 4.8, planned for 18 June. They describe offline map downloads, saved ferry routes, and a new alert when a dock is temporarily closed. The notes say French Canadian is one of three locales in the release, alongside Spanish for Mexico and German. They also say the trip-planning screen has a new “Save for later” action. That wording is in the release notes, but it might not be the final string, so don’t state that the interface already uses it unless the other material confirms that. The build date is presented as planned, not as a release that has already happened.

The glossary export has 46 entries, and the column headings are English source, French Canadian, context, and status. “Ferry terminal” is listed as “terminal de traversier,” status approved, for map labels. “Boarding pass” is “carte d’embarquement,” also approved, for the trip wallet. “Dock” has two entries: “quai” for a place where a ferry boards and “station” in the context of a docked vehicle; that second entry is marked needs review. The glossary says to use “vous” in passenger-facing text. There’s also a note beside “offline”: “Keep the adjective close to the feature name where possible.” I’m not sure if that note applies to the settings screen too, since the context column only says map downloads. Please keep that limitation visible rather than resolving it.

The string sheet is called fr-CA_4.8_round2 and has 312 rows. The completion cell at the top says 287 translated, 19 needs review, and 6 blank. Those are the sheet’s counts; don’t calculate a new percentage. A row for the save action has source “Save for later,” French Canadian “Enregistrer pour plus tard,” and status review. The sheet also contains “Download map for offline use,” translated as “Télécharger la carte pour une utilisation hors ligne,” with approved status. The dock-closure alert is still blank in the sheet. In another row, “Your ferry leaves in 10 min” is translated as “Votre traversier part dans 10 min”; status is translated, not approved. It may be important to distinguish these status labels rather than calling all completed rows approved. The character limit for push alerts is 90, and the sheet has a note that punctuation counts toward that limit.

There is a numbered section in the issue thread titled “Open questions before freeze,” and it has three items. 1. Confirm whether “dock” in the alert means a passenger boarding location or a vehicle docking point. 2. Decide whether the save action should use the glossary’s verb “Enregistrer” or the shorter “Sauvegarder”; the thread says the latter is used in an older web flow, but it is not in the approved glossary. 3. Check whether the temporary-closure alert can fit the 90-character push limit after the final French wording is chosen. These are questions, not decisions. One reviewer wrote, “I can’t approve the alert until we know which dock we mean.” Another person replies that product has been asked, but the thread has no answer from product yet. Please retain that there is a request for clarification and no recorded resolution.

The QA report covers 40 sampled strings on iOS 17.4 and Android 14. It records two layout issues: the saved-route label wraps onto a second line on the smaller iPhone SE screen, and a longer ferry-terminal label clips in the Android map pin at 110% text size. QA says neither issue blocks the build at the moment, but the report marks the Android clipping for follow-up. Don’t turn “not blocking at the moment” into a final sign-off or imply the follow-up is done. The report also says the offline download flow passed on both platforms, while one tester could not reproduce a missing accent seen in an earlier screenshot. That item is marked unable to reproduce, not fixed.

Design’s note is two paragraphs from Mina Laurent. She says the alert icon should stay amber, not red, because the alert is informational unless the ferry operator cancels service. She asks whether the message can say “temporarily unavailable” instead of “closed,” because some docks remain open to pedestrians. The note says this is a wording question for localization and product, not a confirmed change to the English source. It also asks the team to avoid using a wave emoji in the alert because it was removed from the icon set last month. Please don’t suggest it should be added back.

For the summary, make it readable to a release coordinator who has not opened these files. Organize it with a short overview and then a numbered section for the unresolved items; the three thread questions should remain distinguishable, and you can include other open issues there only if the packet supports them. Mention the key glossary and string-sheet details, the build timing and locales, the QA findings, and the design request. Keep the exact quoted reviewer sentence and the quoted English action or alert wording when relevant, without presenting proposed wording as approved. Separate statements in the documents from questions or requests, and note when two sources are about related but different things. Don’t invent a final French translation for the blank alert, decide between the two save verbs, supply product’s missing answer, or claim a release, approval, fix, or sign-off that the packet doesn’t record. A concise but complete summary is fine; the summary itself should not become recommendations or a localization rewrite.", "output": "Create a concise, complete summary of the supplied Harborlight mobile app localization packet for the French Canadian release. Write for a release coordinator who has not read the files. Summarize the packet rather than rewriting its documents or proposing a team plan. Cover the release notes, glossary export, string sheet, localization issue thread, QA report, and design note. Clearly distinguish confirmed statements from questions, requests, and unresolved items; do not imply a question has been answered or a proposed change has been approved.

Start with a short overview. Include build 4.8’s planned date of 18 June, the release locales (French Canadian, Spanish for Mexico, and German), and the features described: offline map downloads, saved ferry routes, and an alert for a temporarily closed dock. Note that “Save for later” appears in the release notes but is not necessarily the final interface wording. Do not describe the planned release as completed.

Summarize the glossary and string-sheet details, including the glossary’s 46 entries and relevant statuses and contexts: approved “terminal de traversier” for map labels and “carte d’embarquement” for the trip wallet; “quai” for a ferry boarding place and “station” for a vehicle docking point, with the latter needing review; and the passenger-facing “vous” guidance. Mention the offline adjective note and that its applicability beyond map downloads is unclear. Report the sheet’s 312 rows and stated counts (287 translated, 19 needing review, 6 blank) without calculating a percentage. Include the save-action row (“Enregistrer pour plus tard,” review), the approved offline-download translation, the blank dock-alert row, and the translated-but-not-approved ferry departure row. Note the 90-character push-alert limit and that punctuation counts toward it.

Then include a numbered section titled “Unresolved items.” Keep the three “Open questions before freeze” items distinct: what “dock” means in the alert; whether to use “Enregistrer” or the older web-flow “Sauvegarder”; and whether the final French alert fits the character limit. Preserve that these are open questions. Include the reviewer’s exact comment, “I can’t approve the alert until we know which dock we mean,” and note that product was asked for clarification but has not answered in the thread. Add other open matters only where supported by the packet.

Also summarize QA’s 40-string sample on iOS 17.4 and Android 14: the iPhone SE saved-route label wraps; the Android map-pin terminal label clips at 110% text size and is marked for follow-up; neither is currently considered build-blocking. The offline-download flow passed on both platforms, and the earlier missing-accent report could not be reproduced. Do not call the follow-up complete, the accent issue fixed, or the report a final sign-off.

Describe Mina Laurent’s design requests: keep the alert icon amber rather than red; consider “temporarily unavailable” instead of “closed” because some docks remain open to pedestrians; and avoid a wave emoji, removed from the icon set last month. Make clear that the wording is a question for localization and product, not a confirmed English-source change. Do not invent a French alert translation, decide between the save verbs, provide product’s missing answer, or claim any unrecorded release, approval, fix, or sign-off. Do not perform the task.", "input": "Please prepare a practical operating procedure and verification checklist for a small warehouse team using handheld barcode scanners during receiving and put-away. The document should help a new employee complete the work consistently, while giving a shift lead enough detail to check that scans and inventory records agree. Keep the guidance specific to the workflow below; do not expand it into a general warehouse safety manual or a proposal for buying equipment.

The warehouse receives cartons from several suppliers at one receiving bay. Each carton has a supplier label and a warehouse item label. The warehouse item label contains a barcode representing the item number; some cartons also have a separate barcode for the lot number. A handheld scanner reads the labels and sends the data to the receiving screen. The employee compares the displayed item and quantity with the packing slip, records the lot number when one is present, and assigns the carton to a storage location. Locations use aisle, bay, and shelf identifiers, such as Aisle 04, Bay 12, Shelf 03. The scanner can display a successful scan, an unreadable-code warning, or a mismatch warning. Wi-Fi is available in the receiving area and most storage aisles, but temporary connection interruptions can occur. Do not assume that every supplier uses the same label layout or that every item has a lot number.

Write instructions for one carton at a time, from the first label check through confirming its put-away location. Explain which label the employee should scan first and how to tell the supplier label apart from the warehouse item label. Include a check that the item number on the receiving screen matches the packing slip before the employee accepts the carton in the system. Clarify that the employee should enter the quantity shown on the packing slip, not infer a quantity from the number of cartons, and should record a lot number only when one is shown and the workflow requests it. If the packing slip and screen do not agree, the employee should stop processing that carton and ask the shift lead to review it rather than choosing a value.

Describe how to scan and verify the storage location after the carton is assigned. The procedure should say to scan the location barcode at the destination and compare the displayed aisle, bay, and shelf with the physical location label before confirming. Include a brief confirmation step so the employee knows whether the carton has been recorded as put away. Do not claim that the system automatically updates any other record unless that behavior is stated here. If the screen does not show a clear confirmation, tell the employee to check with the shift lead before scanning the carton again, to reduce the chance of creating a duplicate transaction.

Please include a numbered section titled “When a scan or connection fails.” Cover an unreadable barcode, a mismatch warning, and a temporary loss of Wi-Fi as separate cases. For an unreadable barcode, have the employee check that the correct label is facing the scanner and try one careful rescan; if it remains unreadable, the employee should set the carton aside and ask the shift lead what to do. For a mismatch, instruct the employee not to override the warning or substitute a different item number. For a connection interruption, explain that the employee should wait for the connection to return and verify the screen state before continuing. The procedure should not promise that an offline scan is saved or that a pending scan will sync later. Include the shift lead as the escalation point, but do not invent a manager, support desk, or approval process.

Add a short section on keeping the carton and its paperwork together while a discrepancy is being reviewed. Include the ordinary workplace reminder, “keep this carton with its packing slip until we know what the screen is showing.” Make clear that this is a temporary handling instruction, not a claim that the discrepancy has been resolved. Explain that employees should report what they observed, such as the item number on the carton, the number displayed on screen, and the warning text, without guessing at the cause.

Finish with a compact shift-lead verification checklist. It should cover whether the employee used the warehouse item label, checked the displayed item against the packing slip, entered the stated quantity, recorded a lot number only when applicable, and verified the aisle, bay, and shelf at the destination. Include a check for a visible put-away confirmation and a reminder to review cartons set aside after warnings or connection problems. Do not define performance targets, error rates, staffing levels, or a required time per carton; none have been provided.

Use plain English, direct action verbs, and short paragraphs. Keep the difference between a required step, a warning, and an escalation clear. Use the labels “Employee” and “Shift lead” where responsibilities need to be distinguished. You may use a short checklist or table if it makes the steps easier to follow, but keep the procedure usable on the warehouse floor and avoid unexplained technical terms. Return only the operating procedure and checklist, with a clear title and the numbered failure-handling section. Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you summarize these notes from a weekday evening at North Wall, an indoor climbing gym? keep it to the events in the notes and don't make it sound like a competition report. i think the most interesting part is how the group handled the route change, so please give that a little attention, but still include the rest. don't guess whether anybody finished the climb.

notes: Lena arrived with her coworker Sam around 6:20 and they checked in for the beginner session. Coach Priya started the group on the blue slab route, which had large footholds and a low overhang. Sam tried first and came down after reaching the marked rest hold. Lena asked if there was another route with less pressure on her wrists. Priya said, “We can switch to the green corner, but it’s steeper.” The group moved there after a short water break. Two people chose to keep trying the blue route instead. Lena watched Priya demonstrate how to turn her hips toward the wall, then tried the green route. The notes say the session ended at 7:35, while several climbers were still taking turns. They don't say who reached the top or whether Lena's wrists felt better afterward.", "output": "Write a concise summary of the supplied notes about a weekday evening beginner session at North Wall, an indoor climbing gym.

Cover the key events, including the group’s initial route, Lena’s request for an alternative, Priya’s response, the move to the green corner, and how the climbers split between routes. Give some attention to how the group handled the route change, while still mentioning the other relevant events. Keep the summary grounded in the notes, do not make it sound like a competition report, and do not guess who reached the top or whether Lena’s wrists felt better afterward."}, {"id": "arka-v3-train-prompt-0198", "row_sha256": "7574b0a465506590f3e119fb3120e74b498586753835575a6e674a990c48dcac", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. i need a set of useful questions for a discussion about indoor climbing. it's for a group with a mix of people who've climbed a lot and people who are pretty new, so the questions should give everyone a way in and not assume that everyone knows the jargon or has done a particular kind of climbing. could cover what makes a session enjoyable or challenging, how people learn and make progress, safety habits and gym etiquette, how routes get set, and the social side of climbing. those are ideas, not separate sections that all need the same number of questions.

please make the questions open enough to get people talking rather than just yes or no, but keep them clear and practical. include a range, from easy starting questions to ones that might lead to a more thoughtful conversation. don't turn this into advice or a guide, and don't give answers to the questions. i want something a facilitator can bring to a group discussion, not a lesson plan or a quiz. keep the focus on indoor climbing and avoid assuming a particular gym, age group, or level of experience.", "output": "Create a set of useful, open-ended questions for a group discussion about indoor climbing. The group includes people with varied experience, from newcomers to frequent climbers, so make the questions accessible without assuming familiarity with jargon or experience with a particular style of climbing.

Include a range of questions, from easy conversation starters to prompts that could lead to more thoughtful discussion. Possible topics include what makes a climbing session enjoyable or challenging, learning and making progress, safety habits, gym etiquette, route setting, and the social side of climbing. These are suggestions, not required sections or quotas. Keep the questions clear and practical, and phrase them to encourage discussion rather than yes-or-no answers.

Provide questions only; do not answer them or turn the response into advice, a guide, a lesson plan, or a quiz. Keep the focus on indoor climbing without assuming a particular gym, age group, or experience level."}, {"id": "arka-v3-train-prompt-0201", "row_sha256": "4727142b7995e3d928c18ef2d29532e95cbe41074d29da0857e44d9a635bb712", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. - In summer, check the water level twice a week.
- If the water level is low, top it up slowly with rainwater.
- Remove fallen leaves with a net.
- Mention that fish should be fed only what they finish in a few minutes.
- Include Mo’s quote: “I check the pump basket every Sunday.”
